contributions.headingText: TP53-associated Li–Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is an autosomal dominant cancer predisposition syndrome caused by germline mutations of the TP53 gene.
Not recommended: sarcoma family syndrome of Li and Fraumeni
TP53-associated LFS is associated with cancers of the breast, soft tissue, bone, brain, adrenal glands, and female genital tract.

LFS is characterized by the early onset of a broad spectrum of cancers and a high lifetime cancer risk. Breast and adrenocortical carcinomas, brain tumours (particularly choroid plexus carcinoma), leukaemia, and soft tissue and bone sarcomas are considered to be the core tumours, which constitute about 70% of LFS-related neoplasms {29076966}. Cancers of the female reproductive organs, in particular ovarian and endometrial carcinomas, occur infrequently {14583457; 28509937}. The expanded clinical definition allows a broader recognition of individuals and families with LFS (see #16235Box #16235) {26014290; 32457520}.

Gynaecological tumours are rare, accounting for 2.7% of cases (57 of 2095 included tumours) in version R19 (August 2018) of the IARC TP53 Database [[IARC TP53 Database [Internet]. Lyon (France): International Agency for Research on Cancer; 2018. Version R19, August 2018. Available from: http://p53.iarc.fr/.]] {27328919}.

LFS is caused by germline mutation of the TP53 gene {1978757; 2259385}. A broad spectrum of TP53 germline mutations involving the coding regions of the gene has been found in families with LFS, but 20–40% of individuals with LFS and the majority of families with Li–Fraumeni–like syndrome may lack detectable mutations {14583457; 12619118}. The lack of 100% concordance between TP53 mutations and the classic LFS phenotype may be explained in several ways, including posttranslational alterations, complete deletion, the effects of modifier genes, and alterations of other genes influencing the phenotype generated by the presence of specific germline alterations {21779515}. Mutations may occur at specific hotspot codons that either interfere with DNA binding or disrupt the structure of the binding surface, thus interfering with its ability to modulate the transcription of target genes {20182602}. Missense mutations lead to a codon change, posing challenges to the functional interpretation of new variants {23161690}. Further mutations may occur outside the DNA-binding domain and include rearrangements and deletions {27984644}. Future studies with novel sequencing technologies such as next-generation sequencing may be able to uncover a higher number of mutations in TP53, as well as in other genes in LFS and Li–Fraumeni–like syndrome {28509937}.

The activation of TP53, one of the most prominent tumour suppressors, leads to protective cellular processes including cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, and senescence to prevent the propagation of genetically altered cells {11099028}, but findings in mouse models have recently challenged the importance of these cellular responses {22682240}. Under normal conditions, the p53 protein is maintained at low levels as a result of rapid turnover mediated by MDM2, its main negative regulator {28254861}. Recent evidence has linked TP53 function to regulation of metabolism and the redox balance to maintain intracellular homeostasis. Cells from individuals with LFS exhibit genomic instability, telomere dysfunction, and spontaneous immortalization {23587008}.

Gynaecological tumours are rare in LFS; they involve the ovaries most frequently, followed by the uterine corpus, the cervix, and the vagina. LFS has been reported in serous carcinoma of the endometrium {22811390} and arising from the fallopian tube, but a second genetic hit seems to be crucial for tumour development {19834951}. A case of concurrent small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type, and pleomorphic liposarcoma of the cervix has been reported {28177947}.
Guidelines for the selection of candidates for TP53 germline testing have recently been updated (see #16235Box #16235).
Essential: pathogenic germline mutation in TP53; appropriate family history.
Stage according to the affected organ site.
